candidates.sentence: One team has 24 move slots, and a Pokemon in this format can learn about 61 moves on average, so a single team has roughly 1,400 one-move neighbours. Scoring all of them at 384 battles each would cost about 527,000 battles, more than three hours on my laptop for a single team, so the study scored three random move edits per team, and the result describes those samples rather than every neighbour.

facts.claim: A team is six Pokemon with up to four distinct moves each, so at most 24 move slots. All 40 starting teams of the edit-kind rerun fill all 24.
facts.source: notes/Teaching/reference/bo-benchmarks-vs-vgc-full-team-search-unit.md, paragraph 'The VGC search unit'; counted from the starting team files ~/vgc-data/edit_kind_rerun/teams/ruggedness/a00.txt to a23.txt and ~/vgc-data/edit_kind_rerun/teams/ruggedness2/s00.txt to s15.txt

facts.claim: The Showdown validator pull for the format gen9championsvgc2026regmb, dated 2026-09-18, lists 14,191 form-move pairs over 232 roster entries. Recomputed from the file: the mean movepool is 14,191 / 232 = 61.2 moves, median 60, range 1 to 105. This is an unweighted mean over every roster entry, not over the Pokemon players actually use.
facts.source: notes/Blog/visuals/team-search-space/domain.json, keys 'format', 'created' and 'roster', each entry's 'pairs' moves taken as a union; matches notes/Teaching/reference/bo-benchmarks-vs-vgc-full-team-search-unit.md, quantity table, column 'Showdown validator pull, 2026-09-18'

facts.claim: Computed: a move edit replaces one move with a legal move that Pokemon does not already know, so 24 x (61.2 - 4) = 1,372 one-move neighbours per team, which rounds to the 1,400 in the sentence. At 384 battles each that is 526,861 battles, 3.4 hours at 43 battles a second.
facts.source: computed from the two facts above, the 384-battle score in v2/FACTS.md, section 'The finished measurement', and the pace in code/docs/top50-one-edit.md, bullet 'Budget'

facts.claim: Counted on the real starting teams with each Pokemon's own validator movepool: the 24 tournament-ready teams have 1,136 to 1,644 one-move neighbours, mean 1,340, and the 16 search-found teams 1,088 to 1,280, mean 1,199. Mega forms were counted with their base form's movepool.
facts.source: computed from domain.json above and the team files in ~/vgc-data/edit_kind_rerun/teams/, which match the plan in ~/vgc-data/edit_kind_rerun/run/results/ruggedness2_shuffled50_parts/vgc_plan.json

facts.claim: What the count leaves out: it counts move edits only, not item, ability, stat alignment, Stat Points or whole-Pokemon edits. It excludes the four moves a Pokemon already knows and treats move order as meaningless. The rerun's move edit drew from a narrower list, moves that are both legal and seen on a training-corpus team, a mean of 47.1 moves over 189 species, which gives about 1,019 move neighbours per tournament-ready team.

facts.claim: Each team got 18 edits, three of each of six kinds, so three of its roughly 1,340 move neighbours were scored, about 0.2 percent.

candidates.sentence: Every score is a win rate over 384 battles against the 50 top-placing tournament teams, about nine seconds of battling on my laptop at 43 battles a second. That budget is why the study gave each of its 40 starting teams 18 random one-edit neighbours, three of each of six edit kinds, out of well over a thousand move edits alone. The whole measurement came to 880 scores and 337,920 battles, a little over two hours.

candidates.sentence: The study changes one thing at a time. A team has roughly 900,000 two-move neighbours, and scoring each at 384 battles would keep my laptop busy for about three months, so this measurement says nothing yet about how two edits combine.
